cues.text: A Faith That Grew Astonishingly Fast
Christianity had arrived in Japan with the missionary St. Francis Xavier in 1549 and spread with remarkable speed under sympathetic local lords' protection.
By the early seventeenth century, the Christian community numbered some three hundred thousand believers among perhaps fifteen to twenty million people.
This growth increasingly alarmed Japan's ruling shoguns, who came to see foreign missionaries as advance agents of Spanish and Portuguese imperial ambition.
Jesuit missionaries who followed Xavier worked with unusual care to adapt Christian teaching to Japanese language and custom.
They won converts even among the powerful samurai class, whose patronage helped the young Church put down roots far faster than in almost any other Asian mission field of the era.
An Edict of Total Expulsion
In 1614, the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu issued a sweeping edict banning Christianity outright.
It ordered all missionaries expelled and all churches destroyed, condemning the foreign faith as a scheme to overthrow right doctrine and seize possession of the land.
The Trampling of Sacred Images
To root out believers who continued to practice in secret, Japanese authorities developed the fumi-e , carved images of Christ or the Virgin.
Suspects were ordered to trample them underfoot to prove their apostasy; those who refused faced execution by methods of calculated cruelty.

These methods included crucifixion, burning, and the infamous "pit," in which the condemned were bound and hung upside down over a shallow grave, often for days, to prolong their suffering as long as possible.

Local officials, required by the shogunate to prove the thoroughness of their searches, sometimes forced entire villages to perform the ritual annually, keeping careful written registers of compliance that survive today as some of the era's most chilling bureaucratic records.
Missionaries Who Would Not Stay Away
Despite the extreme danger, foreign missionaries continued to slip back into Japan disguised as merchants and travelers, ministering in secret to the Christians who remained.
Nearly all were eventually discovered and executed, often alongside the Japanese families who had risked their own lives to shelter them.
The persecution claimed several thousand lives and drove the practice of Christianity in Japan entirely underground for the better part of two and a half centuries.
A Faith Kept Alive in Total Secrecy
Remarkably, Western missionaries were finally permitted to return to Japan in the 1860s, following the end of the country's long isolation.
They discovered thriving communities of Kakure Kirishitan — "hidden Christians."
These communities had secretly preserved baptism, prayer, and fragments of the Catholic liturgy across some seven unbroken generations without a single ordained priest among them.
They passed their faith from parent to child in whispered secrecy for nearly two hundred and fifty years.

Their reappearance, discovered almost by accident when a French missionary priest was approached by villagers near Nagasaki who quietly confided that they shared his faith, remains one of the most moving rediscoveries in the whole history of Christian missions.
Legacy
The persecution in Japan remains, in the memory of the whole Church, one of the most extraordinary demonstrations in Christian history.

It shows a faith's capacity to endure total isolation from its own institutional structures: no bishops, no priests, no sacraments beyond baptism itself, and yet a community that never once let the flame go out.

Their rediscovery in the nineteenth century stands as a permanent and humbling reminder that the Church's true life has never depended, in the last analysis, on anything the world's persecutors could ever fully take away.

Their unbroken, unaided fidelity remains one of the most extraordinary proofs the Church possesses that the sacraments and structures believers rely upon, however necessary, are never quite the whole of what keeps a faith alive.
